chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows one school trip. It starts with a bird that finds its way and a child who faces the rising Sun, then reads the camp, a room, a street map with a bus route, a metro map, an ant's grid and the animals of a zoo. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.title: Videos teach, tools explore
points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student explores, steers, counts and checks the idea alone, with hints, retry and reset. Six tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own plan.

points.title: A tool in three steps
points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own questions, used exactly as the book gives them.

points.title: Every book question has its own video
points.text: Every solved example and every answerable question of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.

points.title: The picture is the mathematics
points.text: Compass roses, street maps, the metro map, the ant's grid and the zoo grid carry each idea. The compass is the same on every board: N at the top, E in red on the right.

points.title: Only the book's pictures and numbers
points.text: Roads, stops, metro lines, grid sizes and the places of animals and foods are the book's own. Any number the plan adds is a practice value and is said to be one.

concepts.concept_name: Four Little Chicks and the Siberian Crane

content.text:
I visited the Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary in Rajasthan and saw an amazing bird called the Siberian Crane!
Wow! Do you know that these birds fly all the way from Siberia, a very cold place, to India?
I wonder how they find their path.
Four Little Chicks of a bird set out to fly,
Spreading their wings they all flew high.
They flew away from East to West,
flew North to South, without any rest.
As they flew and explored the land,
finally, they returned home, hand in hand.
With their mother, they had so much to share,
Our home is the best, beyond compare!

content.text:
1. Predict first: a Siberian Crane flies all the way from Siberia, a very cold place, to India. How could anyone keep track of the way on such a long journey?
2. A friend visited the Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary in Rajasthan and saw an amazing bird, the Siberian Crane. These birds fly all the way from Siberia to India.
3. The children wonder how the cranes find their path. This story does not say. It is a question to wonder about.
4. Now listen to a poem called Four Little Chicks. Four little chicks of a bird set out to fly. They flew away from East to West, and flew North to South, without any rest.
5. As they flew and explored the land, they came back home with their mother. Our home is the best, beyond compare!
6. East, West, North and South are the four directions. Human beings also keep track of directions. One of the ways is by facing the rising Sun. Let's try!

Manu stands on a grassy hill in the morning with his arms stretched out.
Human beings keep track of directions too. One of the ways is by facing the rising Sun.
Turn Manu until he faces the rising Sun, and find which way his left hand, his right hand and his back point.

media.title: Face the Rising Sun

tool_config.title: Face the Rising Sun
tool_config.idea: Find east by turning Manu on the screen until the rising Sun is in front of him, then read the direction of his left hand, his right hand and behind him from that one fact. This is the free first try of the chapter, so it asks and shows; the video that follows names the rule.
tool_config.screen: The sunrise field board on the trip desk, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A round green hill field fills the middle of the board and is the largest thing on screen. Manu, the boy of your maths book, stands in the middle of the field, seen from behind, with both arms stretched out to the sides. At the start the rising Sun is on his right. The rising Sun is a large bright disc fixed low on the horizon above the soft hills, and it never moves when Manu turns. A small arrow grows from his chest to show where he faces, and an arrow grows from each hand, one from his left hand and one from his right hand. Four empty tag slots sit at the end of the front arrow, the left hand arrow, the right hand arrow and behind him, and they turn with him. A tray under the field holds four word tags: North, East, South and West. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with seven progress dots under it. The compass card, a small square card with N at the top, E in red on the right, S at the bottom and W on the left as in your maths book, stays hidden until the practice cards are done and then shows in the top right corner. Controls: Turn left and Turn right (a quarter turn each, with a gentle animation); tap a word tag and then tap a slot to put the tag there, and tap a tag that is in a slot to take it out; Check; Hint; Retry (clears the tags of this card); Reset (returns Manu to his starting turn and clears all the tags); Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a line Where is the Sun now? that says in front of Manu, on his left, on his right or behind him, a count of the quarter turns made, and a card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the picture of the story again: the Siberian Crane that flies all the way from Siberia, the four little chicks of the poem that fly from east to west and from north to south, and Manu standing on the hill with his arms stretched out. Read the line: Human beings also keep track of directions. One of the ways is by facing the rising Sun. Then turn Manu until he faces the rising Sun, and press Next.

Turn Manu until the Sun is in front of him and tag that direction, tag the direction of his left hand and of his right hand, turn him to face north (practice values) and tag the hands again, turn him back to the Sun and tag the direction behind him, then open the compass card and compare.

Manu's own lines from your maths book, unchanged, as an open challenge: Manu is facing the rising Sun. That direction is ___. His left hand is pointing in the ___ direction. His right hand is pointing in the ___ direction. Then: which way is west? Fill the tags and read what the tool shows. The video that follows names the rule.
challenges: Card 1: turn Manu until the rising Sun is straight in front of him. Which direction tag goes in front of him? Answer: East, because the Sun rises in the east.
Card 2: with Manu facing the Sun, tag his left hand and his right hand. Answer: North for his left hand and South for his right hand.

Card 3 (practice values): turn Manu to face north, one quarter turn to the left from the Sun. Which direction does his right hand point to, and which his left hand? Answer: his right hand points to the East and his left hand to the West. The Sun is on his right now, and his hands point in other directions than before, so a hand does not always point the same way.
Card 4: turn Manu back to face the rising Sun, one quarter turn to the right, and tag the direction behind him. Answer: West, which is opposite to East.

Card 5: open the compass card and compare. Manu faces East, so on the card he looks to the right. Which tags match the card? Answer: all four. East is in front of him on the right of the card, North is at the top on his left hand, South is at the bottom on his right hand and West is on the left behind him.

Challenge: 'Manu is facing the rising Sun. That direction is ___. His left hand is pointing in the ___ direction. His right hand is pointing in the ___ direction.' Turn Manu to the Sun and fill the three tags. Answer: East, North, South.

Challenge: 'which way is west?' Tag the direction that is neither in front of Manu nor on a hand. Answer: West is behind Manu, opposite to the rising Sun. Next stop: the rule that names the four directions.
feedback: Turn left and Turn right move Manu a quarter turn each time. The Sun stays where it is, so the line Where is the Sun now? changes as he turns, for example from on his right to in front of him.
When the Sun is not in front of Manu on card 1 the tool says: The Sun is not in front of Manu yet. Turn him again.
When he faces the Sun the tool says: Manu faces the rising Sun, so the tag in front of him is East. The slot lights up soft green when its tag is right.

A wrong tag shows a soft amber note and never a red cross, for example: Look again. Face the Sun yourself and stretch out your left arm. Which direction does it point to? The tool names the right tag only after the second try.
After card 3 the tool says: Manu faces north, so his left hand points West now. A hand does not always point the same way. It depends on which way Manu faces.
The last card is an open challenge: the tool shows what the tags say and lets the student change them, and the video that follows names the rule.
tool_config.done_when: Manu has been turned to the rising Sun, the tags East, North, South and West have been placed for his front, his left hand, his right hand and behind him, the compass card has been opened and compared, and the two questions from your maths book have been answered with the tags.

The Sun rises in the east. When Manu faces the Sun, he faces east. Now think about his hands: which side is each hand on?
Manu faces east. Face the Sun yourself and stretch out your left arm: it points north. Then stretch out your right arm: it points south.
The tool turns Manu to the Sun and puts East in front of him, North on his left hand, South on his right hand and West behind him. Then a similar card follows for you to try.

concepts.concept_name: Finding Directions by the Rising Sun

content.text: Human beings also keep track of directions. One of the ways we figure out directions is by facing the rising Sun. Let's try!
content.publication_text: Human beings also keep track of directions. One of the ways we figure out directions is by facing the rising Sun. Let's try!
lines: Human beings also keep track of directions. One of the ways we figure out directions is by facing the rising Sun. Let's try!

content.text:
1. Predict first: it is early morning and you stand facing the rising Sun. Which of the four directions are you facing?
2. You are facing east. The Sun rises in the east, so facing the rising Sun is facing east.
3. Now stretch your arms out to the sides. Your left hand points north and your right hand points south.
4. West is behind you. West is opposite to east, and south is opposite to north.
5. Watch out: your left hand does not always point west. Turn to face north and your left hand points west. The directions stay where they are. Only your hands turn with you.
6. A compass rose shows the four directions: N for north at the top, E for east on the right in red, S for south at the bottom and W for west on the left.
7. Say the four names aloud: north, east, south, west. A compass is another way to find directions.
8. Rule: face the rising Sun and you face east. Your left hand is north, your right hand is south and west is behind you.

content.text:
Worked example: Lali faces the rising Sun on the school ground. She then turns to face the direction her left hand was pointing to. Which direction is she facing now, and which direction is behind her?
1. Lali faces the rising Sun. The rising Sun is in the east, so she faces east.
2. Facing east, her left hand points north and her right hand points south.
3. She turns to face the direction her left hand was pointing to. That is north, so she now faces north.
4. Behind her is the opposite of north. North and south are opposite directions, so south is behind her.
5. Check: north is at the top of the compass rose and south is at the bottom, so they are opposite directions.
Answer: She is facing north, and south is behind her

7. Rule: on a picture whose compass has N at the top, above is north, below is south, right is east and left is west.

5. North of the sandpit: look above the sandpit. The swing is there.
6. Check: the swing and the slide are in the top row and the sandpit and the seesaw are in the bottom row, and the top row is north of the bottom row.
Answer: The slide is east of the swing, the seesaw is south of the slide, the sandpit is west of the seesaw and the swing is north of the sandpit

content.text:
Worked example: A girl stands at the centre of a room plan with a compass, N at the top. A table is above her, a bed is to the right of her, a door is below her and a cupboard is to the left of her. Say the direction of each thing from the girl. Then say in which direction the girl is from the bed.

2. The table is above her, so the table is north of her.
3. The bed is to the right of her, so the bed is east of her.
4. The door is below her, so the door is south of her.
5. The cupboard is to the left of her, so the cupboard is west of her.
6. Now stand at the bed and look at the girl. She is to the left of the bed, so she is west of the bed.
7. Check: the bed is east of the girl and the girl is west of the bed, and east and west are opposite directions.
Answer: The table is north, the bed east, the door south and the cupboard west of the girl. From the bed the girl is to the west

tool_config.title: Direction Clues
tool_config.idea: The direction of a thing depends on what it is said from. Moving a compass cross onto the lake, onto a playground thing and onto the girl shows which things are north, south, east and west of that place, and colouring and placing tents turns direction clues into actions.
tool_config.screen: Three boards on the trip desk, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The main board shows the bird-watching camp seen from above, as in your maths book: a grey road that curves from the top down to the bottom left, a lake with four ducks in the lower middle, four white tents with small red flags (one on the left of the road, one near the top on the right of the road, one just above the lake and one below the lake) and many green and yellow trees. The camp is the largest thing on screen. Two more boards slide in when a card needs them: the girl's room as in your maths book, with the girl, the window, the bed, the cupboard and the bedside table, and a small playground with a swing at the top left, a slide at the top right, a sandpit at the bottom left and a seesaw at the bottom right (practice values). The compass card, a small square card with N at the top, E in red on the right, S at the bottom and W on the left, sits in the top right corner of every board. A movable compass cross, a small round card with two diagonal lines through its centre, splits the picture around it into four zones: north above, south below, east on the right and west on the left. When the cross rests on a thing, the four zones are tinted softly and each zone shows its letter at the edge. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with seven progress dots under it, and a clue strip under it shows the clue being worked on. A pen tray holds a blue, a green, a purple and a yellow pen, and one spare tent waits beside the camp board. On the room board a small tray holds the word tags North, East, South and West, and a notes card with four lines, East, West, North and South, takes the names of things in the student's own room. Controls: drag the compass cross onto a thing; tap a thing to read its zone; tap a tent and then a pen to colour it, and tap the tent again to clear its colour; drag the spare tent onto the board; drag a word tag next to a name in the room list; type on the notes card; Check; Hint; Retry (clears the colours, tags or tent of this card); Reset (restores the board); Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a zone line that says, after a tap, which zone of the cross the tapped thing is in, for example The slide is in the east zone of the cross; a count of tents coloured out of 4; and a card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the compass card and remember: facing the rising Sun is facing east, and on every picture N is at the top. Put the compass cross on the lake. Which tent is to its north?

With the cross on the lake, name the tent to its north and the tent to its south; on the playground (practice values) put the cross on the swing and find the thing to its east, on the sandpit and find the thing to its north, and on the slide and find where the swing is from it.

Your maths book's own items, unchanged. Bird Watching: colour the tents with the four clues (the tent to the west of the road is blue, the tent closest to the lake is green, the tent north of the green tent is purple, the tent south of the lake is yellow) and draw a tent to the east of the lake. Map of a Room: write the directions of the window, the bed, the cupboard and the bedside table in relation to the girl, make a drawing of your room, and write the names of the things placed in the east, west, north and south.
challenges: Card 1: put the compass cross on the lake. Which tent is to the north of the lake and which tent is to the south of it? Answer: the tent just above the lake is to its north and the tent below the lake is to its south.

Card 2 (practice values): on the playground board put the cross on the swing. Which thing is east of the swing? Then put the cross on the sandpit. Which thing is north of the sandpit? Answer: the slide is east of the swing, and the swing is north of the sandpit.

Card 3 (practice values): put the cross on the slide. In which direction is the swing from the slide? Answer: west. The slide is east of the swing, so the swing is west of the slide. Seen from the other thing, the direction is the opposite one.

Challenge: 'Children are at a bird-watching camp. Read the clues and colour the tents in the camp accordingly. The tent to the west of the road is blue. The tent closest to the lake is green. The tent north of the green tent is purple. The tent south of the lake is yellow.' Answer: blue is the tent on the left of the road, green is the tent just above the lake, purple is the tent above the green tent near the top, and yellow is the tent below the lake.

Challenge: 'Now, draw a tent to the east of the lake.' Drag the spare tent onto the board. Answer: sample answer, the tent goes on the ground to the right of the lake. Any place to the right of the lake is right. Your answer may differ.

Challenge: 'Write the directions of the following in relation to the girl. Window ___ Bed ___ Cupboard ___ Bedside table ___' Drag the tags next to the names. Answer: sample answer, window north, bed east, cupboard west, bedside table south. The cupboard and the bedside table sit between two directions, so we name the nearest one. Your answer may differ.

Challenge: 'Make a drawing of your room and locate the direction in which different things have been placed in relation to you standing at the centre of the room. Make the direction arrow for your room.' Then: 'Write the names of the things that are placed in the following directions. East ___ West ___ North ___ South ___' Draw on paper, then type the names on the notes card. Answer: sample answer, in a sample room the bed is in the east, the cupboard in the west, the window in the north and the door in the south. To find north in your own room, face the rising Sun, which is east: north is on your left hand. Your answer may differ.
feedback: When the cross rests on a thing the four zones tint and the zone line says where a tapped thing is, for example: The slide is in the east zone of the cross. The swing is in the west zone of the cross when the cross is on the slide.
A tent coloured to a clue clicks in with a soft chime and the clue strip says why, for example: The tent closest to the lake is the one just above it. That tent is green.
A wrong colour shows a soft amber note and never a red cross, for example: Which tent is west of the road? West is to the left on the picture. The tool names the right tent only after the second try.

A tag dropped next to a name in the room list is read at once, for example: The window is on the back wall, above the girl: north. A tag between two directions gets the note: This thing sits between two directions. Name the nearest one.
The spare tent turns green when it stands to the right of the lake, with the note: This tent is east of the lake. A tent anywhere else slides back with: East is to the right on the picture.
Open items, the tent to the east of the lake, the room list, the drawing and the names, are never marked wrong: the tool says Your answer may differ and offers Next.

media.title: Reading Directions on a Picture
media.context: Maps and Locations. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show how to read directions on a picture with a compass: north at the top, east to the right, and find what lies north, south, east or west of an object. It works this example: A playground picture has a compass with N at the top. A swing is at the top left, a slide at the top right, a sandpit at the bottom left and a seesaw at the bottom right. Which thing is east of the swing, south of the slide, west of the seesaw and north of the sandpit?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a picture has a compass with N at the top. A boat is drawn above a bridge. Is the boat north, south, east or west of the bridge? The boat is north of the bridge. The top of the picture is north. Read the compass first. N is at the top, S at the bottom, E on the right and W on the left. A thing drawn above another thing is north of it. Below is south. To the right is east. To the left is west. Try it on a playground: a swing at the top left, a slide at the top right, a sandpit at the bottom left and a seesaw at the bottom right. The slide is to the right of the swing, so the slide is east of the swing. Always begin from one thing and look in a direction. East of the swing is the slide. West of the seesaw is the sandpit. Rule: on a picture whose compass has N at the top, above is north, below is south, right is east and left is west. 1. The compass has N at the top, so above is north, below is south, the right is east and the left is west. 2. East of the swing: look to the right of the swing. The slide is there. 3. South of the slide: look below the slide. The seesaw is there. 4. West of the seesaw: look to the left of the seesaw. The sandpit is there. 5. North of the sandpit: look above the sandpit. The swing is there. 6. Check: the swing and the slide are in the top row and the sandpit and the seesaw are in the bottom row, and the top row is north of the bottom row. Answer: The slide is east of the swing, the seesaw is south of the slide, the sandpit is west of the seesaw and the swing is north of the sandpit

media.title: Directions from Where You Stand
media.context: Maps and Locations. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show that the direction of a thing is said from a person standing at a place, for example the centre of a room, and that if one thing is east of another then the other is west of it. It works this example: A girl stands at the centre of a room plan with a compass, N at the top. A table is above her, a bed is to the right of her, a door is below her and a cupboard is to the left of her. Say the direction of each thing from the girl. Then say in which direction the girl is from the bed.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a girl stands at the centre of a room plan with N at the top. A shelf is on the wall above her. Which direction is the shelf from the girl, and which direction is the girl from the shelf? The shelf is north of the girl. From the shelf, the girl is south of it. The direction of a thing is always said from somewhere, from a person or from a place. We say the direction in relation to that person or place. Look at the room plan from the girl's place at the centre. Above her is north, to the right of her is east, below her is south and to the left of her is west. Name the things you find. Now turn the question round. If the bed is east of the girl, then the girl is west of the bed, not east. East and west are opposite directions. To find north in your own room, face the rising Sun. That is east. North is on your left hand. Rule: say what is in each direction while you stand at the centre. If A is east of B, then B is west of A. 1. N is at the top, so above is north, the right is east, below is south and the left is west. 2. The table is above her, so the table is north of her. 3. The bed is to the right of her, so the bed is east of her. 4. The door is below her, so the door is south of her. 5. The cupboard is to the left of her, so the cupboard is west of her. 6. Now stand at the bed and look at the girl. She is to the left of the bed, so she is west of the bed. 7. Check: the bed is east of the girl and the girl is west of the bed, and east and west are opposite directions. Answer: The table is north, the bed east, the door south and the cupboard west of the girl. From the bed the girl is to the west
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students say which object is north, south, east or west of another object on a picture with a compass, reading the top of the picture as north and the right as east.
Students write the direction of things in a room from a girl standing at the centre, and say that if one thing is east of another then the other is west of it.

Students use clues about directions to colour four tents, draw a tent east of the lake, write the direction of things in a room from the girl, and name things in the four directions of their own room.

Window: it is on the back wall, behind the girl, so it is north of her.
Bed: it is on the right side of the picture, so it is east of her.
Cupboard: it is on the back wall at the left, a little behind her, so the nearest direction is west.

Check: the cupboard and the bedside table sit between two directions. We use only four directions, so we name the nearest one. Your answer may differ.

1. Predict first: you stand at the Basketball Court on the street map and walk down the map, across Market Road. Which place do you reach first?
2. You reach the Shopping Centre. The compass beside the map has S at the bottom, so down the map is south. The Shopping Centre is south of the Basketball Court.

8. Rule: on a street map up is north, down is south, right is east and left is west, and the dotted line shows the route.

content.text:
Worked example: What is just south of the Basketball Court, across Market Road, and what is just north of it?
1. A street map is a picture of roads and places seen from above. The compass has N at the top, E on the right, S at the bottom and W on the left.
2. Find the Basketball Court in the middle of the map. Market Road runs along the bottom of the court.
3. Go down the map, across Market Road. Down the map is south, so the place just south of the Basketball Court is the Shopping Centre.
4. Now go up the map from the court, across the small road above it. Up the map is north, so just north of the court is the block with the pond and Jaideep's House.
5. Turn it round. If the Shopping Centre is south of the court, then the court is north of the Shopping Centre.
6. Check with the compass: up is N, so north is up the map and south is down the map.
Answer: The Shopping Centre is just south of the Basketball Court. The block with the pond and Jaideep's House is just north of it.

concepts.concept_name: Turning Right and Left on a Route

content.text:
1. Predict first: a bus is driving north and takes a right turn. Which direction is it driving now: east, south or west?
2. East. A turn says which hand you turn towards. A direction says where you are going. They are two different things.
3. Face north and hold out your arms. Your right hand points east and your left hand points west. A right turn takes you towards your right hand.
4. A right turn changes north to east, east to south, south to west and west to north.
5. A left turn changes the direction the other way round: north to west, west to south, south to east and east to north.
6. A right turn does not always make a bus drive east. A bus that is driving east and turns right drives south.
7. To read a route, say two things at every turn: right or left, and the direction after the turn.
8. Rule: a right turn takes the direction through north, east, south, west in that order. A left turn takes it through north, west, south, east.

content.text:
Worked example: A cycle drives north along a road and turns left at a junction. Which direction is it driving after the turn? At the next junction it turns left again. Which direction is it driving now?
1. The cycle drives north. Face north: your left hand points west and your right hand points east.
2. A left turn is a turn towards the left hand. The left hand points west, so after the first turn the cycle drives west.
3. Now the cycle drives west. Face west: your left hand points south.
4. The second left turn is towards south, so the cycle now drives south.
5. Check with the rule: a left turn takes north to west, and west to south.
6. The two left turns together made the cycle drive the opposite way to the way it started: it started north and now drives south.
Answer: After the first left turn the cycle drives west. After the second left turn it drives south
content.publication_text:
Worked example: A cycle drives north along a road and turns left at a junction. Which direction is it driving after the turn? At the next junction it turns left again. Which direction is it driving now?
1. The cycle drives north. Face north: your left hand points west and your right hand points east.
2. A left turn is a turn towards the left hand. The left hand points west, so after the first turn the cycle drives west.
3. Now the cycle drives west. Face west: your left hand points south.
4. The second left turn is towards south, so the cycle now drives south.
5. Check with the rule: a left turn takes north to west, and west to south.
6. The two left turns together made the cycle drive the opposite way to the way it started: it started north and now drives south.
Answer: After the first left turn the cycle drives west. After the second left turn it drives south

media.description: Concept video: Show how to read a street map: roads and places seen from above, the compass, the stops and a dotted route. It works this example: What is just south of the Basketball Court, across Market Road, and what is just north of it?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: you stand at the Basketball Court on the street map and walk down the map, across Market Road. Which place do you reach first? You reach the Shopping Centre. The compass beside the map has S at the bottom, so down the map is south. The Shopping Centre is south of the Basketball Court. A street map is a picture of roads and places seen from above. Roads have names, like Hospital Road, Market Road and Park Road. The school bus will take the children to the Qutb Minar in Delhi, and then they will go to the zoo by a metro train. The bus picks up children from Stop 1 (S1) and Stop 2 (S2), marked on the map. The compass shows the directions on the map. N is at the top, E in red is on the right, S is at the bottom and W is on the left. The red dotted line is the route of the bus. Follow it with your finger and read the name of each road it uses. Look at the map and talk about it. Which places are near each other? Which way is one place from another? Ask your own questions by looking at the map. Rule: on a street map up is north, down is south, right is east and left is west, and the dotted line shows the route. 1. A street map is a picture of roads and places seen from above. The compass has N at the top, E on the right, S at the bottom and W on the left. 2. Find the Basketball Court in the middle of the map. Market Road runs along the bottom of the court. 3. Go down the map, across Market Road. Down the map is south, so the place just south of the Basketball Court is the Shopping Centre. 4. Now go up the map from the court, across the small road above it. Up the map is north, so just north of the court is the block with the pond and Jaideep's House. 5. Turn it round. If the Shopping Centre is south of the court, then the court is north of the Shopping Centre. 6. Check with the compass: up is N, so north is up the map and south is down the map. Answer: The Shopping Centre is just south of the Basketball Court. The block with the pond and Jaideep's House is just north of it.

media.description: Concept video: Show how a right turn or a left turn changes the direction a vehicle is driving: right turn from north gives east, left turn from north gives west. It works this example: A cycle drives north along a road and turns left at a junction. Which direction is it driving after the turn? At the next junction it turns left again. Which direction is it driving now?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a bus is driving north and takes a right turn. Which direction is it driving now: east, south or west? East. A turn says which hand you turn towards. A direction says where you are going. They are two different things. Face north and hold out your arms. Your right hand points east and your left hand points west. A right turn takes you towards your right hand. A right turn changes north to east, east to south, south to west and west to north. A left turn changes the direction the other way round: north to west, west to south, south to east and east to north. A right turn does not always make a bus drive east. A bus that is driving east and turns right drives south. To read a route, say two things at every turn: right or left, and the direction after the turn. Rule: a right turn takes the direction through north, east, south, west in that order. A left turn takes it through north, west, south, east. 1. The cycle drives north. Face north: your left hand points west and your right hand points east. 2. A left turn is a turn towards the left hand. The left hand points west, so after the first turn the cycle drives west. 3. Now the cycle drives west. Face west: your left hand points south. 4. The second left turn is towards south, so the cycle now drives south. 5. Check with the rule: a left turn takes north to west, and west to south. 6. The two left turns together made the cycle drive the opposite way to the way it started: it started north and now drives south. Answer: After the first left turn the cycle drives west. After the second left turn it drives south

content.question: The bus will start from the parking area. It will go north and then it will take a right turn onto ___ Road driving in the ___ direction to reach Stop 1 (S1).

content.book_number: Bus Route: Stop 1
content.question: The bus will start from the parking area. It will go north and then it will take a right turn onto ___ Road driving in the ___ direction to reach Stop 1 (S1).
steps: Find the PARKING area at the bottom of the map. The red dotted route goes up the map from there, and up the map is north.
Near the top of the map the route meets the road with the Hospital above it. The name on that road is Hospital Road.
The bus drives north and takes a right turn. A right turn changes north to east, so the bus drives east along Hospital Road.
Stop 1 is at the hospital gate on Hospital Road, so the bus reaches Stop 1 driving east.
Check: the red arrows on Hospital Road point to the right, and the compass has E on the right.
content.answer: The blanks are Hospital and east. The bus turns right onto Hospital Road driving east.

The route now goes down the map. Down the map is south.
The bus changes from driving east to driving south. A right turn changes east to south, so the turn is a right turn.
Stop 2 is beside the Shopping Centre, near the south end of Park Road, so the bus reaches Stop 2 driving south.
Check: facing east, your right hand points south.
content.answer: The blanks are right, Park and south. The bus turns right onto Park Road driving south.

Turn right and go east along Hospital Road to Park Road. The Children's Park is on the east side of Park Road, at the top right.

content.book_number: Street Map: the stop closer to Lali's house
content.question: Which stop is closer to Lali's house? ___
steps: Find Lali's House at the top left of the map.
Find the two stops. Stop 1 is at the hospital gate on Hospital Road, near the top of the map. Stop 2 is beside the Shopping Centre, near the bottom right.

concepts.concept_name: Reading a Metro Map: Lines, Stations and Key

content.text:
Children will get off the bus at the Qutb Minar metro station. To reach the zoo, they need to get off the metro at the Supreme Court metro station.
Here is the metro map for your reference.
Read the key to the symbols and identify them on the map.

content.text:
1. Predict first: at Hauz Khas the map does not show a plain circle but a capsule with a yellow dot and a magenta dot. What do you think the two dots tell you?
2. The two dots tell you that two lines meet at that station, the Yellow Line and the Magenta Line. Here you can change from one line to the other.
3. Read the key. It numbers 10 symbols. Symbols 1 to 8 are the coloured lines: Red, Yellow, Blue, Airport Express, Green, Violet, Pink and Magenta.
4. Symbol 9, a plain circle, is a Metro Station. Symbol 10, a capsule with two coloured dots, is an Interchange Line, a place where two lines meet.
5. Each coloured line is a different metro route. The colours make it easier to find and follow a route on the map.
6. Observe the map carefully. The children get off the bus at the Qutb Minar metro station, and to reach the zoo they get off the metro at the Supreme Court metro station. Find both names on the map.
7. Rule: a coloured line is one metro route, a circle is a metro station, and a capsule with two coloured dots is an interchange where those two lines meet.

content.text:
Worked example: On the metro map, look at Hauz Khas. Which two lines meet there, and how do you know you can change lines there?
1. Find Hauz Khas in the lower middle of the metro map. Its symbol is not a plain circle. It is a capsule with two coloured dots.
2. The two dots are yellow and magenta. In the key, the yellow colour is the Yellow Line and the magenta colour is the Magenta Line.
3. Now read the key. Symbol 9, a plain circle, is a Metro Station. Symbol 10, a capsule with two coloured dots, is an Interchange Line.
4. So Hauz Khas is an interchange. The Yellow Line and the Magenta Line meet there, and you can change from one line to the other.
5. Check: the capsule has two dots, one dot for each line that meets there.
Answer: The Yellow Line and the Magenta Line meet at Hauz Khas. Its symbol is the interchange capsule from the key, so you can change lines there

content.text:
1. Predict first: you ride from Hauz Khas to Kalkaji Mandir and on to Badarpur. When you count the stations between, do you count Hauz Khas and Badarpur?
2. No. The stations between are only the ones strictly between the two ends. Hauz Khas and Badarpur are the ends, so we do not count them.
3. Count every station between the two ends, one by one. A capsule is a station too, so it counts as one, whether you change there or ride past it.
4. To change lines, get off at a capsule that shows the colours of both lines. At Kalkaji Mandir the capsule has a magenta dot and a violet dot, so you can change from the Magenta Line to the Violet Line there.
5. Two lines can cross on the map without a capsule. Then there is no interchange, and you cannot change lines at that crossing.
6. To count a route with a change, count the stations on the first line, then the capsule where you change, then the stations on the next line.
7. Rule: count the circles between the two ends, count a capsule as one station, do not count the two ends, and change lines only at a capsule.

content.text:
Worked example: Ride the Magenta Line from Hauz Khas to Kalkaji Mandir, change to the Violet Line and ride on to Badarpur. How many stations are between Hauz Khas and Kalkaji Mandir, and between Kalkaji Mandir and Badarpur?
1. Start at Hauz Khas and ride along the Magenta Line towards Kalkaji Mandir. Count only the circles between the two stations, not the two ends.
2. There are 4 circles between Hauz Khas and Kalkaji Mandir, so 4 stations between them.
3. Kalkaji Mandir is a capsule with a magenta dot and a violet dot. The Magenta Line and the Violet Line meet there, so we change lines at Kalkaji Mandir.
4. Now ride along the Violet Line towards Badarpur. There are 6 circles between Kalkaji Mandir and Badarpur, so 6 stations between them.
5. In all, between Hauz Khas and Badarpur there are 4 stations, then Kalkaji Mandir, then 6 stations: 4 + 1 + 6 = 11 stations.
6. Check: the capsule counts as one station, and we did not count Hauz Khas or Badarpur, the two ends.
Answer: There are 4 stations between Hauz Khas and Kalkaji Mandir, and 6 between Kalkaji Mandir and Badarpur. In all, 4 + 1 + 6 = 11 stations between Hauz Khas and Badarpur

tool_config.title: Metro Route Planner
tool_config.idea: Read the metro map as a network: ride a coloured line, change lines only at a capsule that shows both colours, and read the counter of stations between two stations, counting every circle and capsule between the two ends but not the ends.
tool_config.screen: A station information board on the trip desk, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The Delhi metro map of your maths book is the largest thing on screen: eight coloured lines (Red, Yellow, Blue, Airport Express, Green, Violet, Pink and Magenta), circles for stations, capsules for interchanges, and the station names that are printed on the map, such as Qutb Minar, Hauz Khas, INA, Rajiv Chowk, Supreme Court, Mayur Vihar and Botanical Garden. A key panel beside the map lists the 10 symbols of the key: the 8 coloured lines, 9 Metro Station (a plain circle) and 10 Interchange Line (a capsule with two coloured dots). A route card at the right lists the lines used and the stations where the lines change. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: tap a start station and an end station; tap a line colour in the key panel to ride along that line, and a thick highlight in that colour grows along the line; tap a capsule to change line; a Mark switch that puts an orange ring on a tapped station; a Save route button that keeps up to 3 routes on the route card; answer cards that click into an answer strip; Undo (takes back the last ride), Clear route, Check, Hint, Retry (clears the route of this question), Reset (clears the whole board), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a counter stations between that updates with every circle or capsule passed, not counting the two ends, a changes count and the list of change stations on the route card, and a card number out of 7.
student_does: The video's strip with Hauz Khas, where the Yellow Line and the Magenta Line meet. Find the capsule on the map. Which two lines meet there?

Match the key symbols to their names, ride the Blue Line and the Pink Line and read the counter, tap a crossing of two lines that has no capsule, and ride a line past a capsule that counts as one station.

The book's own metro questions: what the coloured lines represent, marking the Qutb Minar and Supreme Court stations, tracing different routes between them, Lali's suggestion, the route with the fewest stations, and the best way to the zoo.
challenges: Card 1: match the key. Drag the names to the symbols: a plain circle and a capsule with two coloured dots. Answer: the plain circle is a Metro Station and the capsule with two coloured dots is an Interchange Line.
Card 2 (practice values): ride the Blue Line from Mayur Vihar to Botanical Garden and read the counter. Answer: 5 stations between, not counting Mayur Vihar and Botanical Garden.
Card 3 (practice values): ride the Pink Line from INA to Mayur Vihar and read the counter. Answer: 5 stations between. The capsule where the Pink Line meets the Violet Line counts as one of the 5.

Card 4: tap the place where the Airport Express Line crosses the Magenta Line. Can you change lines there? Answer: no. There is no capsule, so the lines only cross. You can change lines only at a capsule that shows both colours.
Card 5 (practice values): ride the Yellow Line from Hauz Khas to Central Secretariat. The capsule at INA counts as one station. How many stations are between? Answer: 2 + 1 + 3 = 6 stations between.

Challenge: 'What do the different coloured lines represent?' and 'Mark the Qutb Minar station on the Yellow Line and the Supreme Court station on the Blue Line.' Build the first answer from the cards and mark the two stations with rings. Answer: each coloured line is a different metro route; Qutb Minar is the labelled circle on the lower part of the Yellow Line, next to Saket, and Supreme Court is the labelled circle on the Blue Line, the third station after Rajiv Chowk.

Challenge: (a) 'Look at the metro map and trace different routes from the Qutb Minar metro station to the Supreme Court metro station.' (b) 'Lali says, "We can take the Yellow Line and change the metro at Hauz Khas to take the Magenta Line." If the children follow Lali's suggestion, at which station(s) do they need to change the metro line again to reach the Supreme Court metro station?' (c) 'Which route has the least number of stations between Qutb Minar and Supreme Court?' (d) 'Which metro route(s), do you think, is/are the best way to reach the zoo from Qutb Minar?' Answers: (a) Sample answer: Route A, the Yellow Line to Rajiv Chowk and then the Blue Line, 14 stations between and 1 change; Route B, the Yellow Line to INA, the Pink Line to Mayur Vihar and then the Blue Line, 15 stations between and 2 changes; Route C, the Yellow Line to Hauz Khas, the Magenta Line to Botanical Garden and then the Blue Line, 25 stations between and 2 changes. (b) Botanical Garden, where the Magenta Line meets the Blue Line. (c) Route A, with 14 stations between. (d) Sample answer: Route A, because it has the fewest stations (14) and only one change, at Rajiv Chowk. Your answer may differ.
feedback: Each ride highlights the part of the line in its own colour and the counter updates at once, for example: Between Mayur Vihar and Botanical Garden there are 5 stations, not counting the two ends.
A tap on a capsule shows its two colours and offers the change, for example: Hauz Khas shows yellow and magenta, so you can change from the Yellow Line to the Magenta Line here.
A tap on a crossing without a capsule gives a soft amber note: You can change lines only where the capsule shows both colours. Here the lines only cross.
A route that stops before the end station says where it stopped, for example: This route stops at Hauz Khas. Keep riding until you reach Supreme Court.
A count that includes the two ends shows a clue, for example: Do not count the first and the last station. Count only the circles between them.
Open questions, the routes and the best way, are never marked wrong when every change is at a capsule that shows both colours: the tool says Your answer may differ and offers Next.

media.description: Concept video: Show how to read a metro map: coloured lines are routes, circles are stations, a capsule with two coloured dots is an interchange where one can change lines. It works this example: On the metro map, look at Hauz Khas. Which two lines meet there, and how do you know you can change lines there?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: at Hauz Khas the map does not show a plain circle but a capsule with a yellow dot and a magenta dot. What do you think the two dots tell you? The two dots tell you that two lines meet at that station, the Yellow Line and the Magenta Line. Here you can change from one line to the other. Read the key. It numbers 10 symbols. Symbols 1 to 8 are the coloured lines: Red, Yellow, Blue, Airport Express, Green, Violet, Pink and Magenta. Symbol 9, a plain circle, is a Metro Station. Symbol 10, a capsule with two coloured dots, is an Interchange Line, a place where two lines meet. Each coloured line is a different metro route. The colours make it easier to find and follow a route on the map. Observe the map carefully. The children get off the bus at the Qutb Minar metro station, and to reach the zoo they get off the metro at the Supreme Court metro station. Find both names on the map. Rule: a coloured line is one metro route, a circle is a metro station, and a capsule with two coloured dots is an interchange where those two lines meet. 1. Find Hauz Khas in the lower middle of the metro map. Its symbol is not a plain circle. It is a capsule with two coloured dots. 2. The two dots are yellow and magenta. In the key, the yellow colour is the Yellow Line and the magenta colour is the Magenta Line. 3. Now read the key. Symbol 9, a plain circle, is a Metro Station. Symbol 10, a capsule with two coloured dots, is an Interchange Line. 4. So Hauz Khas is an interchange. The Yellow Line and the Magenta Line meet there, and you can change from one line to the other. 5. Check: the capsule has two dots, one dot for each line that meets there. Answer: The Yellow Line and the Magenta Line meet at Hauz Khas. Its symbol is the interchange capsule from the key, so you can change lines there

media.title: Changing Lines and Counting Stations
media.context: Maps and Locations. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show how to ride one line, change at an interchange and count the stations between two stations, not counting the two ends. It works this example: Ride the Magenta Line from Hauz Khas to Kalkaji Mandir, change to the Violet Line and ride on to Badarpur. How many stations are between Hauz Khas and Kalkaji Mandir, and between Kalkaji Mandir and Badarpur?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: you ride from Hauz Khas to Kalkaji Mandir and on to Badarpur. When you count the stations between, do you count Hauz Khas and Badarpur? No. The stations between are only the ones strictly between the two ends. Hauz Khas and Badarpur are the ends, so we do not count them. Count every station between the two ends, one by one. A capsule is a station too, so it counts as one, whether you change there or ride past it. To change lines, get off at a capsule that shows the colours of both lines. At Kalkaji Mandir the capsule has a magenta dot and a violet dot, so you can change from the Magenta Line to the Violet Line there. Two lines can cross on the map without a capsule. Then there is no interchange, and you cannot change lines at that crossing. To count a route with a change, count the stations on the first line, then the capsule where you change, then the stations on the next line. Rule: count the circles between the two ends, count a capsule as one station, do not count the two ends, and change lines only at a capsule. 1. Start at Hauz Khas and ride along the Magenta Line towards Kalkaji Mandir. Count only the circles between the two stations, not the two ends. 2. There are 4 circles between Hauz Khas and Kalkaji Mandir, so 4 stations between them. 3. Kalkaji Mandir is a capsule with a magenta dot and a violet dot. The Magenta Line and the Violet Line meet there, so we change lines at Kalkaji Mandir. 4. Now ride along the Violet Line towards Badarpur. There are 6 circles between Kalkaji Mandir and Badarpur, so 6 stations between them. 5. In all, between Hauz Khas and Badarpur there are 4 stations, then Kalkaji Mandir, then 6 stations: 4 + 1 + 6 = 11 stations. 6. Check: the capsule counts as one station, and we did not count Hauz Khas or Badarpur, the two ends. Answer: There are 4 stations between Hauz Khas and Kalkaji Mandir, and 6 between Kalkaji Mandir and Badarpur. In all, 4 + 1 + 6 = 11 stations between Hauz Khas and Badarpur

steps: Count the stations between Qutb Minar and Supreme Court on each route. A capsule where we change counts as one station. Do not count Qutb Minar or Supreme Court.

Route A: count the circles on the Yellow Line from Qutb Minar to Hauz Khas (2), Hauz Khas (1), then 2 to INA, INA (1), 3 to Central Secretariat, Central Secretariat (1), 1 to Rajiv Chowk, Rajiv Chowk (1), then 2 on the Blue Line to Supreme Court. 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 14.
Route B: 5 stations from Qutb Minar to INA, INA (1), 5 on the Pink Line to Mayur Vihar, Mayur Vihar (1), 1 to Yamuna Bank, Yamuna Bank (1), 1 to Supreme Court. 5 + 1 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 15.

Route C: 3 stations from Qutb Minar to Hauz Khas, 4 on the Magenta Line to Kalkaji Mandir, Kalkaji Mandir (1), 7 to Botanical Garden, Botanical Garden (1), 5 on the Blue Line to Mayur Vihar, Mayur Vihar (1), 1 to Yamuna Bank, Yamuna Bank (1), 1 to Supreme Court. 3 + 4 + 1 + 7 + 1 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 25.
14 is less than 15, and 15 is less than 25, so Route A has the fewest stations between.
Check: Route A changes at Rajiv Chowk, the capsule where the Yellow Line meets the Blue Line, so it stays on the Yellow Line the longest.
content.answer: Route A: the Yellow Line to Rajiv Chowk, then the Blue Line. It has 14 stations between, fewer than Route B (15) and Route C (25).

media.description: Question video: Which route has the least number of stations between Qutb Minar and Supreme Court?
media.teaching_notes: 1. Count the stations between Qutb Minar and Supreme Court on each route. A capsule where we change counts as one station. Do not count Qutb Minar or Supreme Court. 2. Route A: count the circles on the Yellow Line from Qutb Minar to Hauz Khas (2), Hauz Khas (1), then 2 to INA, INA (1), 3 to Central Secretariat, Central Secretariat (1), 1 to Rajiv Chowk, Rajiv Chowk (1), then 2 on the Blue Line to Supreme Court. 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 14. 3. Route B: 5 stations from Qutb Minar to INA, INA (1), 5 on the Pink Line to Mayur Vihar, Mayur Vihar (1), 1 to Yamuna Bank, Yamuna Bank (1), 1 to Supreme Court. 5 + 1 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 15. 4. Route C: 3 stations from Qutb Minar to Hauz Khas, 4 on the Magenta Line to Kalkaji Mandir, Kalkaji Mandir (1), 7 to Botanical Garden, Botanical Garden (1), 5 on the Blue Line to Mayur Vihar, Mayur Vihar (1), 1 to Yamuna Bank, Yamuna Bank (1), 1 to Supreme Court. 3 + 4 + 1 + 7 + 1 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 25. 5. 14 is less than 15, and 15 is less than 25, so Route A has the fewest stations between. 6. Check: Route A changes at Rajiv Chowk, the capsule where the Yellow Line meets the Blue Line, so it stays on the Yellow Line the longest. Answer: Route A: the Yellow Line to Rajiv Chowk, then the Blue Line. It has 14 stations between, fewer than Route B (15) and Route C (25).

A sample map and its key are given below.
Gate, Road, Building, Tank, Hidden Objects, Wall, Fence, Seat/Bench, Path, Garden, Tree

content.text:
1. Predict first: your friend sees a long rectangle on your map. How can your friend know that it means a shelf and not a table?
2. Your friend needs a key. A key is a box on the map that shows each symbol and says what it means.
3. A map uses symbols, small simple drawings, for the things in a place seen from above. Look at the sample map in your maths book. Its key shows symbols for Gate, Road, Building, Tank, Hidden Objects, Wall, Fence, Seat or Bench, Path, Garden and Tree.
4. The key of the sample map shows a red circle for Hidden Objects, a thick hatched line for a Wall and a line with small ticks for a Fence.
5. To make your own map, first draw the place from above. Then choose one symbol for each kind of thing, and write each symbol in the key with its name.
6. To hide something, choose a place on the map and mark it with a red dot. Then give your friend a clue that uses directions, like: start at the door and walk north.
7. Rule: every symbol on a map is explained in the key, and a hidden thing is marked with a red dot.

content.text:
Worked example: Make a map of a library corner seen from above: 2 shelves on the west wall, 1 table with 4 chairs in the middle, and the door on the south wall. Make a key, and hide a bookmark with a red dot.
1. Draw the floor of the corner from above as a large rectangle. With N at the top, the west wall is the left side and the south wall is the bottom side.
2. Draw 2 long rectangles along the west wall, one for each shelf. A long rectangle is the symbol for a shelf.
3. Draw 1 square in the middle for the table and 4 small squares around it for the 4 chairs.
4. Draw a gap in the south wall for the door.
5. Hide the bookmark under the table and mark it with a red dot.
6. Make the key. A long rectangle means shelf. A square with 4 small squares around it means table and chairs. A gap in the wall means door. A red dot means the hidden bookmark.
7. Read the map to find the bookmark: start at the door on the south wall, walk north to the table, and look under it.
8. Check: every symbol on the map is in the key, and there is 1 red dot.
Answer: The map has 2 shelves, a table with 4 chairs and a door, a key that explains each symbol, and a red dot under the table. From the door, walk north to the table to find the bookmark

concepts.concept_name: Pull it together and do it: Our School Map

content.text:
A map is a picture of a place seen from above. It uses symbols for the things in the place.
The key tells what each symbol means. Every symbol on the map must be in the key.
Mark a hidden thing with a red dot or a red flag.
Give a clue with directions: start at the gate and walk east to the tree.

content.question: Make a map showing the different places in your school. Make a key for the symbols used in the map. Hide some objects in these places. Mark the positions where things are hidden with red dots or flags. Now, challenge your friends to find the hidden things by reading the map.

content.question: Make a map showing the different places in your school. Make a key for the symbols used in the map. Hide some objects in these places. Mark the positions where things are hidden with red dots or flags. Now, challenge your friends to find the hidden things by reading the map.
steps: Choose the places to show. In this sample school there is a gate in the west wall, a road along the west side, a building on the east side, a tree and a bench near the middle, and a garden near the south wall on the west side.

Draw the school from above with N at the top, and draw one symbol for each kind of place. For example a rectangle with two squares for the building, a long rectangle for the bench, a cloud shape for the tree.
Make the key: a small box that shows each symbol with its name, gate, road, building, tree, seat or bench, garden, and the red dot for a hidden object.
Hide 3 objects: one beside the bench, one beside the tree and one in the garden. Mark each place with a red dot.
Write a challenge for a friend: start at the gate and walk east to the tree. The hidden object is a little south of the tree.
Check: every symbol on the map is in the key, there are 3 red dots, and the clue uses only north, east, south and west.
Your map will be different: use your own school, your own symbols and your own clue.
content.answer: Sample answer: a map with a key and 3 red dots. Clue: start at the gate, walk east to the tree. The object is a little south of it. Your map will be different.

content.text:
The arrows show the direction in which the ant can move.
Fill in the blanks below with the distances and the directions in which the ant must move from its starting position.

content.text:
1. Predict first: an ant stands on a grid point. A leaf lies 4 squares away along a grid line, on the west side. Each square is 1 cm. How far must the ant crawl, and in which direction?
2. The ant can crawl only along the lines of the grid. The arrows show the direction in which it can move, and the compass tells you which way is north, east, south and west.
3. Count the squares along the line. 4 squares of 1 cm each are 4 cm, so the leaf is 4 cm towards the west.
4. A distance always comes with a direction. 6 cm towards the south is not the same place as 6 cm towards the north.
5. Some food is not on one straight line. Take a berry 2 squares to the east and 4 squares to the north. The ant crawls 2 cm towards the east, turns, and crawls 4 cm towards the north. Each straight part is a leg. This path has two legs and its length is 2 + 4 = 6 cm.
6. Say a path as a list of legs: 2 cm towards the east, then 4 cm towards the north.
7. Rule: each square is 1 cm. Count the squares in a straight line for the distance, say the direction, and write a path with turns as one leg after another.

content.text:
Worked example: An ant starts from its anthill, a grid point of a grid of 1 cm squares. A leaf is 4 squares to the west. A seed is 6 squares to the south. A berry is 2 squares to the east and then 4 squares to the north. How far, and in which direction, must the ant crawl to reach each one?
1. Each square of the grid is 1 cm. Count the squares along a grid line to find a distance.
2. Leaf: count 4 squares to the west. The ant crawls 4 cm towards the west.
3. Seed: count 6 squares to the south. The ant crawls 6 cm towards the south.
4. Berry: it is not on one straight line. First count 2 squares to the east, then turn and count 4 squares to the north.
5. The path has two legs: 2 cm towards the east, then 4 cm towards the north.
6. Length of the path: 2 + 4 = 6 cm.
7. Check: 4 squares are 4 cm and 6 squares are 6 cm. The two legs of the berry path are 2 squares and 4 squares, and 2 + 4 = 6 squares, which is 6 cm.
Answer: Leaf: 4 cm towards the west. Seed: 6 cm towards the south. Berry: 2 cm towards the east, then 4 cm towards the north, 6 cm in all

content.text:
1. Predict first: a berry is 4 cm to the east and 3 cm to the north of the ant. The ant can go east first or north first, or even wander a little. Which routes along the grid lines are the shortest?
2. Route 1: crawl 4 cm towards the east, then 3 cm towards the north. The length is 4 + 3 = 7 cm.
3. Route 2: crawl 3 cm towards the north, then 4 cm towards the east. The length is 3 + 4 = 7 cm. The same length, in a different order.
4. Route 3: crawl 5 cm towards the east, then 3 cm towards the north, then 1 cm towards the west. The length is 5 + 3 + 1 = 9 cm. The step towards the west is a step the wrong way, and it adds length.
5. The shortest routes are 7 cm. They go only towards the berry, east and north, and never west or south.
6. Turns do not decide the length. Try 2 cm east, 1 cm north, 2 cm east, then 2 cm north. It has three turns. Its length is 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 7 cm, so it is a shortest route too. Count the cm, not the turns.
7. Rule: the shortest route goes only towards the food. A step the wrong way adds to the length.

content.text:
Worked example: A berry is 4 cm to the east and 3 cm to the north of the ant. Route 1: 4 cm east, then 3 cm north. Route 2: 3 cm north, then 4 cm east. Route 3: 5 cm east, then 3 cm north, then 1 cm west. Find the length of each route. Which routes are the shortest?
1. Route 1 has two legs, 4 cm east and 3 cm north. Length: 4 + 3 = 7 cm.
2. Route 2 has two legs, 3 cm north and 4 cm east. Length: 3 + 4 = 7 cm.
3. Route 3 has three legs, 5 cm east, 3 cm north and 1 cm west. Length: 5 + 3 + 1 = 9 cm.
4. Routes 1 and 2 are both 7 cm. Route 3 is 9 cm, which is 2 cm longer.
5. Route 3 goes 1 cm towards the west, away from the berry, and so it also needs 1 cm more towards the east. These two extra steps make the 2 cm.
6. Check: the berry is 4 cm east and 3 cm north, and 4 + 3 = 7. A route that goes only east and north cannot be shorter than 7 cm.
Answer: Routes 1 and 2 are 7 cm and are the shortest. Route 3 is 9 cm, because it goes 1 cm the wrong way

media.title: Ant Path

tool_config.title: Ant Path
tool_config.idea: Build a path on a grid one square at a time and read it as legs, each with a distance in cm and a direction, then compare routes to the same food by their lengths: the shortest route goes only towards the food.
tool_config.screen: The ant grid board on the trip desk, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A friendly wooden desk holds one large board: a grid of 11 by 11 squares, each square 1 cm, as in your maths book. The grid is the largest thing on screen. A compass card sits in the top left corner of the grid with N at the top, E in red on the right, S at the bottom and W on the left, and the label 1 cm with a small double arrow sits in the top right corner. A small ant stands on a grid point near the middle. In the book challenges the four foods sit where your maths book puts them: a plate of laddoos 2 squares to the right of the ant, a pile of sugar 3 squares above it, a slice of bread 3 squares to the left and 2 squares below it, and an apple 3 squares to the right and 3 squares below it. In the practice cards the foods are replaced by a leaf, a seed and a berry that the tool places (practice values). In the book challenges the red dashed route drawn in your maths book is shown as a faint guide to follow. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: four large arrow buttons N, E, S and W on the right of the board, and each one moves the ant 1 cm along the grid line and draws a red dashed trail with small arrowheads behind it; Undo takes back the last cm; Clear trail puts the ant back on its start and removes the trail; Save route keeps the trail as a named route for comparing; Compare routes shows two saved routes side by side; a legs card with a number box and a direction chip (north, east, south or west) for each leg, with Add leg and Remove leg, where the answer is written; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the trail and the legs card of this step), Reset (puts the ant back and empties the saved routes), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the legs list that the tool writes as the ant moves (for example 3 cm east, then 3 cm south), a length counter in cm (for example Length: 6 cm), the direction of the ant's last move, and, in Compare routes, the two lengths and a line such as Route B is 2 cm longer.
student_does: Look at the small practice grid from the video, with the ant and a berry. Tap E two times to move the ant 2 cm towards the east, the first leg of the way to the berry, and read the legs list.
Use the arrow buttons to move the ant to the practice foods, read the legs list and the length counter each time, and save two routes to one berry to compare their lengths.

The book's own questions on the grid of your maths book: how far, and in which direction, the ant crawls to the laddoos, to the sugar, to the bread and to the apple, and the other routes to the apple with the shortest one.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): a leaf lies 4 cm to the west of the ant. Move the ant to the leaf with the arrow buttons. What does the legs list say, and how long is the path? Answer: 4 cm west, and the length is 4 cm, because 4 squares of 1 cm each are 4 cm.

Card 2 (practice values): a berry lies 2 cm to the east and 4 cm to the north of the ant. Move the ant to the berry and read the legs list and the length. Answer: 2 cm east, then 4 cm north, and the length is 2 + 4 = 6 cm.

Card 3 (practice values): a berry lies 4 cm to the east and 3 cm to the north. Build Route A, 4 cm east then 3 cm north, and save it. Build Route B, 5 cm east, 3 cm north, then 1 cm west, and save it. Press Compare routes. Answer: Route A is 4 + 3 = 7 cm and Route B is 5 + 3 + 1 = 9 cm, so Route A is 2 cm shorter. Route B has a step 1 cm the wrong way.

Card 4 (practice values): the berry is still 4 cm east and 3 cm north. Build a route with more turns: 2 cm east, 1 cm north, 2 cm east, then 2 cm north. Is it shorter than Route A, longer, or the same? Answer: the same. Its length is 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 7 cm. It has three turns but it never goes the wrong way, so it is a shortest route too.

Challenge: 'To get to the laddoos, the ant has to crawl how far, and towards which direction? Each square of the grid is 1 cm.' Then: 'To get to the sugar, the ant has to crawl ___ cm in the ___ direction.' Then: 'To get to the bread, the ant has to crawl ___ cm in the ___ direction; then ___ cm in the ___ direction.' Move the ant with the arrow buttons, then fill the legs card. Answers: the laddoos: 2 cm towards the east. The sugar: 3 cm in the north direction. The bread: 3 cm in the west direction; then 2 cm in the south direction (5 cm in all).

Challenge: 'To get to the apple, the ant needs to crawl ___ cm towards ___, and then ___ cm towards ___, and finally ___ cm towards ___.' Then: 'Identify other routes to reach the point where apple is located. Which one is the shortest?' Answers: the apple: 5 cm towards south, 3 cm towards east, and finally 2 cm towards north, which is 5 + 3 + 2 = 10 cm in all. Sample answer for the other routes: 3 cm east then 3 cm south (6 cm); 3 cm south then 3 cm east (6 cm); 1 cm south, 3 cm east, then 2 cm south (6 cm). The shortest routes are 6 cm, and the route in your maths book is 10 cm. Your routes may differ.
feedback: Every tap moves the ant 1 cm and adds to the trail. The legs list joins moves in the same direction into one leg, for example: 3 cm east, then 3 cm south.
The length counter adds the cm of all the legs, for example 3 + 3 = 6, and shows it as Length: 6 cm.
If the ant is not on the food yet, a soft amber note says how far is left and which way, for example: The sugar is 1 cm more towards the north.

A wrong number or direction on the legs card shows a soft amber note that points at the first thing to look at, for example: Count the squares on this leg again. Up is north. The tool shows the expected leg only after the second try.

In Compare routes the tool writes the two lengths and why they differ, for example: Route A is 7 cm and Route B is 9 cm. Route B is 2 cm longer because it has a step 1 cm towards the west, away from the berry.

The other routes to the apple are open answers and are never marked wrong: the tool checks that each route ends on the apple, reads its length, says whether it is a shortest route, and says: Your answer may differ.
tool_config.done_when: The student has moved the ant to the practice foods and read their legs and lengths, compared two routes to one berry, written the legs for the laddoos, the sugar, the bread and the apple, and named the shortest routes to the apple.

media.description: Concept video: Show how a path on a grid of 1 cm squares is a list of distances in cm and directions. It works this example: An ant starts from its anthill, a grid point of a grid of 1 cm squares. A leaf is 4 squares to the west. A seed is 6 squares to the south. A berry is 2 squares to the east and then 4 squares to the north. How far, and in which direction, must the ant crawl to reach each one?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: an ant stands on a grid point. A leaf lies 4 squares away along a grid line, on the west side. Each square is 1 cm. How far must the ant crawl, and in which direction? The ant can crawl only along the lines of the grid. The arrows show the direction in which it can move, and the compass tells you which way is north, east, south and west. Count the squares along the line. 4 squares of 1 cm each are 4 cm, so the leaf is 4 cm towards the west. A distance always comes with a direction. 6 cm towards the south is not the same place as 6 cm towards the north. Some food is not on one straight line. Take a berry 2 squares to the east and 4 squares to the north. The ant crawls 2 cm towards the east, turns, and crawls 4 cm towards the north. Each straight part is a leg. This path has two legs and its length is 2 + 4 = 6 cm. Say a path as a list of legs: 2 cm towards the east, then 4 cm towards the north. Rule: each square is 1 cm. Count the squares in a straight line for the distance, say the direction, and write a path with turns as one leg after another. 1. Each square of the grid is 1 cm. Count the squares along a grid line to find a distance. 2. Leaf: count 4 squares to the west. The ant crawls 4 cm towards the west. 3. Seed: count 6 squares to the south. The ant crawls 6 cm towards the south. 4. Berry: it is not on one straight line. First count 2 squares to the east, then turn and count 4 squares to the north. 5. The path has two legs: 2 cm towards the east, then 4 cm towards the north. 6. Length of the path: 2 + 4 = 6 cm. 7. Check: 4 squares are 4 cm and 6 squares are 6 cm. The two legs of the berry path are 2 squares and 4 squares, and 2 + 4 = 6 squares, which is 6 cm. Answer: Leaf: 4 cm towards the west. Seed: 6 cm towards the south. Berry: 2 cm towards the east, then 4 cm towards the north, 6 cm in all

media.title: Finding the Shortest Route
media.context: Maps and Locations. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show that several routes reach the same point and that the shortest routes never take a step away from it. It works this example: A berry is 4 cm to the east and 3 cm to the north of the ant. Route 1: 4 cm east, then 3 cm north. Route 2: 3 cm north, then 4 cm east. Route 3: 5 cm east, then 3 cm north, then 1 cm west. Find the length of each route. Which routes are the shortest?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a berry is 4 cm to the east and 3 cm to the north of the ant. The ant can go east first or north first, or even wander a little. Which routes along the grid lines are the shortest? Route 1: crawl 4 cm towards the east, then 3 cm towards the north. The length is 4 + 3 = 7 cm. Route 2: crawl 3 cm towards the north, then 4 cm towards the east. The length is 3 + 4 = 7 cm. The same length, in a different order. Route 3: crawl 5 cm towards the east, then 3 cm towards the north, then 1 cm towards the west. The length is 5 + 3 + 1 = 9 cm. The step towards the west is a step the wrong way, and it adds length. The shortest routes are 7 cm. They go only towards the berry, east and north, and never west or south. Turns do not decide the length. Try 2 cm east, 1 cm north, 2 cm east, then 2 cm north. It has three turns. Its length is 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 7 cm, so it is a shortest route too. Count the cm, not the turns. Rule: the shortest route goes only towards the food. A step the wrong way adds to the length. 1. Route 1 has two legs, 4 cm east and 3 cm north. Length: 4 + 3 = 7 cm. 2. Route 2 has two legs, 3 cm north and 4 cm east. Length: 3 + 4 = 7 cm. 3. Route 3 has three legs, 5 cm east, 3 cm north and 1 cm west. Length: 5 + 3 + 1 = 9 cm. 4. Routes 1 and 2 are both 7 cm. Route 3 is 9 cm, which is 2 cm longer. 5. Route 3 goes 1 cm towards the west, away from the berry, and so it also needs 1 cm more towards the east. These two extra steps make the 2 cm. 6. Check: the berry is 4 cm east and 3 cm north, and 4 + 3 = 7. A route that goes only east and north cannot be shorter than 7 cm. Answer: Routes 1 and 2 are 7 cm and are the shortest. Route 3 is 9 cm, because it goes 1 cm the wrong way

media.teaching_notes: 1. Find where the apple is. It is 3 squares to the right of the ant and 3 squares below it: 3 cm towards the east and 3 cm towards the south. 2. Check: any route made of 3 cm east and 3 cm south, in any order, is 6 cm. Your answer may differ. Answer: Sample answer: 3 cm east then 3 cm south, or 3 cm south then 3 cm east. concepts.concept_name: Reading a Position: Column and Row

content.text:
Children observe a map of the zoo drawn on a grid. Each vertical line (column) and horizontal line (row) is marked with a number.
First move horizontally from 0 and then vertically.
We write the meeting point of the first row and the first column as (1,1).

content.text:
1. Predict first: the zoo map is drawn on a grid with a number on every line. To find the giraffe you start at 0. Do you walk east first or north first?
2. Each vertical line is a column and each horizontal line is a row, and every line has a number. The numbers belong to the lines, and an animal stands where a column line and a row line meet.
3. Start at 0, the corner at the bottom left. First move horizontally towards the east along the bottom, counting the column lines, until you reach column 8. That is 8 steps east.
4. Then move vertically towards the north, counting the row lines, until you reach row 9. That is 9 steps north. The giraffe stands at this meeting point.
5. We write the two numbers in a bracket with the column first and the row second: (8,9). In the same way the meeting point of column 1 and row 1 is (1,1).
6. Rule: start at 0, first move east to the column, then north to the row, and write (column,row).

content.text:
Worked example: Find the position of the giraffe on the zoo map. Start from 0, move east to the 8th column, then move north to the 9th row. How do we write the position?
1. Start at 0, the corner at the bottom left of the grid.
2. Move east along the bottom line, counting the numbered column lines 1, 2, 3 up to 8. Stop at column 8. That is 8 steps east.
3. From there move north along the column line, counting the row lines 1, 2, 3 up to 9. Stop at row 9. That is 9 steps north.
4. The giraffe stands where column 8 and row 9 meet.
5. Write the column first and the row second: (8,9).
6. Check: 8 steps east first, then 9 steps north, and the bracket (8,9) lists the column and then the row.
Answer: The giraffe is at (8,9): 8 steps east, then 9 steps north

concepts.concept_name: The Order of the Two Numbers

content.text:
1. Predict first: you walk 8 steps east and 9 steps north to the giraffe. A friend walks 9 steps east and 8 steps north. Does the friend reach the giraffe?
2. No. The friend reaches a different meeting point, (9,8), a spot on the path where no animal stands.
3. The first number tells the steps east, the column. The second number tells the steps north, the row. So (8,9) and (9,8) are two different places.
4. To read a position, say it as a walk: first east, then north.
5. Rule: the first number is always the column, the second number is always the row.

content.text:
Worked example: A child says that the giraffe is at (9,8). Is that right?
1. The giraffe stands at (8,9): 8 steps east, then 9 steps north.
2. (9,8) means 9 steps east, then 8 steps north. That is a different meeting point.
3. Walk it on the map: start at 0, move east to column 9, then north to row 8. This is a spot on the path, and no animal stands there.
4. The first number is the column and the second number is the row, so changing the order changes the place.
5. Check: (8,9) is the giraffe and (9,8) is not, so (8,9) and (9,8) are not the same place.
Answer: No. The giraffe is at (8,9). (9,8) is 9 steps east and 8 steps north, a spot with no animal
